milestones.notes: async/await/suspend/resume/promise keywords added in 0.2.0 ("stackless coroutines"); reworked into allocator-free "async functions" in 0.5.0. Broke when the self-hosted compiler shipped as the ONLY compiler in 0.11.0 ("Async functions regressed with the release of 0.11.0", per the 0.12.0 notes, citing LLVM's inability to optimize them and async function pointers preventing stack size from being known). The keywords were formally removed from the grammar in 0.15.1 ("it is settled that there will not be async/await keywords in the language"). Reintroduced conceptually as a library-level API in 0.16.0's std.Io interface (Io.async, Future(T), .await, .cancel) -- a colorblind-async model, not new syntax.

stage2 (self-hosted, written in Zig) became the DEFAULT compiler in 0.10.0; the old C++ "stage1" bootstrap compiler remained available behind -fstage1 for code stage2 didn't support yet (notably async/await). stage1 was deleted entirely in 0.11.0 ("the C++ implementation of Zig was deleted"), leaving stage2 -- now bootstrapped via a 2.4 MiB WebAssembly binary plus a C compiler -- as the only compiler.

build.zig.zon + the new ZON (Zig Object Notation) data format debuted in 0.11.0 ("the debut of Package Management"). No central registry: packages are arbitrary directory trees, tarballs, or git URLs pinned by content hash. Still described in 0.11.0's own notes as usable mainly for "simple pure-Zig projects"; optional dependencies and first-class binary-dependency support were still only planned.

"zig cc"/"zig c++" expose Zig's bundled Clang as a cross-compiling C/C++ compiler; the underlying capability (Zig ships libc for many targets, so it can link/cross-compile C code) existed since 0.4.0. The ergonomic zig cc subcommand with full Clang CLI-flag compatibility -- popularized by the blog post "zig cc: a Powerful Drop-In Replacement for GCC/Clang" -- arrived in 0.6.0.

Opt-in and experimental via the -fincremental flag starting in 0.14.0 ("not ready to be enabled by default"; completeness varies by linker backend and compiler-state serialization isn't implemented, so it must be paired with --watch and -fno-emit-bin). 0.15.x called it "stable enough" only for that no-emit workflow, still with "known bugs" that "can lead to miscompilations". Not on by default as of 0.16.0.

std.http.Client debuted in 0.11.0 as a dependency of the package manager's URL fetcher (transfer-encoding: chunked, redirects, connection pooling/keep-alive). It is HTTP/1.1 only; no HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 client exists as of 0.16.0. The HTTP stack was reworked in 0.12.0 (std.http.Headers removed, server rewritten) and again in 0.15.1 ("Writergate", moved onto the new std.Io.Writer/Reader interfaces).

std.crypto.tls shipped a TLS 1.3-only client in 0.11.0 (built to support the HTTP client/package manager). No TLS 1.2 fallback, no server implementation, and at launch "there is not yet any automated testing for this API, so use it at your own risk". Still client-only and 1.3-only as of 0.16.0.

std.os.spawnThread (later std.Thread.spawn) added in 0.3.0, using pthreads when linking libc and raw syscalls otherwise, "works on all targets". Zig has never had a GIL. In 0.16.0 the higher-level primitives built on std.Thread (Mutex, Condition, ResetEvent, WaitGroup, Futex, RwLock, Semaphore) were superseded by std.Io equivalents, and std.Thread.Pool was removed outright in favor of std.Io.Group/async.
arm64-linux (Shawn Landden's port) reached Tier 2 in 0.4.0; blocked from Tier 1 by lack of CI at the time. It is STILL Tier 2, not Tier 1, as of 0.16.0's support table.

0.8.0's new self-hosted linker gained the ability to generate well-formed, codesigned arm64 (Apple Silicon) macOS binaries and to cross-compile C/C++/Zig to them, though 0.9.0's notes admit "we don't have any CI coverage for this target yet". aarch64-macos is STILL Tier 2, not Tier 1, as of 0.16.0.
0.9.0 published the first-ever ARM64 Windows build, explicitly flagged as untested ("Zig developers are still in the process of acquiring the hardware"). Remains Tier 2 through 0.16.0.

comptime-parameterized functions and types (Zig's approach to generics) were part of the language from the first public beta; there was never a pre-generics era to graduate from, unlike languages that bolted generics on later.

os_support.windows: i386 and x86_64 standard-library target support; no stated minimum OS version
os_support.macos: i386 and x86_64 standard-library target support; no arm64 (Apple Silicon did not exist)
os_support.linux: x86_64 standard-library target support; freestanding (no OS abstraction) mode additionally covers arm, aarch64, mips, powerpc, s390x, sparc, thumb, bpf, hexagon, r600, amdgcn, spir, lanai

added: manual memory management, no GC, no hidden control flow

no zig build system yet (0.2.0)
no zig fmt yet (0.3.0)
no formal Tier support table yet (introduced 0.4.0)
no self-hosted compiler roadmap public yet (self-hosted became default 0.10.0)
no package manager (added 0.11.0)

os_support.windows: no formal tier table yet; targeted alongside Linux/macOS
os_support.linux: no formal tier table yet; self-hosted compiler work begins targeting it first

added: error sets and error return traces
limitations: coroutines are "brand-spanking new" with no documentation or non-trivial examples yet
goto removed in favor of labeled loops/blocks/break/continue
no zig fmt yet (0.3.0)
no Tier support table yet (0.4.0)
self-hosted compiler and package manager both years away

added: std.os.spawnThread: real OS threads on all targets (pthreads with libc, raw syscalls without)

added: formal Tier system (1-4) and Support Table introduced

only Tier 1 targets "thoroughly tested"; other libcs planned but not present

added: Async Functions reworked: allocator-free, non-generic, inferred from suspend points, frame supplied by the caller

no package manager
iOS and Android support brand new and lower-tier

os_support.macos: 10.13+ unchanged; target-specific OS version ranges (min AND max) introduced

added: "zig cc" gains full Clang command-line-flag compatibility ("a Powerful Drop-In Replacement for GCC/Clang")
zig-bootstrap tarball for building LLVM/Clang/LLD/Zig from source with no branching logic

limitations: Windows 7 no longer supported (8.1+ required)
self-hosted compiler still not the default
no package manager
zig cc still recommended only as a low-level escape hatch; --c-source / build-system API preferred

added: self-hosted compiler (stage2) becomes the primary development focus and driver code, though .zig files are still compiled by stage1 by default
C header file generation tracked as a roadmap item
limitations: self-hosted compiler (stage2) still cannot be used for normal builds (stage1 remains default until 0.10.0)
no package manager (tracked as roadmap "Package Manager Status")

added: Self-hosted compiler (stage2) becomes the DEFAULT compiler; old C++ bootstrap ("stage1") still available behind -fstage1 for those not ready to upgrade
limitations: async/await "is not done yet" in the self-hosted compiler -- users of async/await cannot upgrade to stage2 until it's complete (it never was; async regressed permanently in 0.11.0)
stage2 has fresh bugs, missing or less-helpful compile errors, and "falls short of stage1" on C ABI compatibility, C translation, several codegen backends, and the self-hosted linker (MachO/COFF/ELF)
macOS 10 (Catalina) no longer supported
still no package manager

os_support.other: FreeBSD, OpenBSD, NetBSD, WASI, UEFI, Plan9 each get dedicated support sections

added: Package manager debut: build.zig.zon + ZON format, std.Build.dependency/addModule/anonymousDependency
stage1 (the C++ compiler) DELETED entirely; stage2 becomes the ONLY compiler, bootstrapped via a 2.4 MiB WebAssembly file plus a C compiler
std.http.Client (HTTP/1.1; used by the package manager to fetch URLs; chunked transfer-encoding, redirects, connection pooling/keep-alive)
limitations: async functions regressed with this release and were never fixed in the self-hosted compiler (LLVM cannot optimize them well; async function pointers prevent the stack size from being known)

package manager has no official registry and no optional dependencies or first-class binary-dependency support yet

added: Reworked std.http (std.http.Headers removed, server rewritten from scratch)

limitations: Async/Await formally flagged as an unresolved roadmap item: "their future in the Zig language is unclear" due to LLVM optimization limits and async-function-pointer stack-size problems
"Bring-Your-Own-OS API Layer Regressed"
package manager still pre-1.0, usable mainly for "simple pure-Zig projects"

os_support.windows: 10+; Windows DLLs now install to <prefix>/bin/ by default

added: BatBadBut command-injection mitigation for process spawning
ComptimeStringMap renamed to StaticStringMap and enhanced
std.zip / zip-archive support usable from build.zig.zon
limitations: small release focused on stdlib renames and a security fix rather than new capability

os_support.windows: 10+ (no dedicated OS-version table published this cycle; last explicit minimum was 0.13's Windows 10+)
os_support.macos: 11+ (same caveat; dedicated OS-version-requirements table introduced next release, 0.15.1)

added: Incremental Compilation: opt-in experimental via -fincremental (recommended with file-system watching; backend-dependent completeness)
Multithreaded backend support: some compiler backends can now run in parallel with semantic analysis
ZON parsing/serialization as a language feature (not just build.zig.zon)
limitations: incremental compilation not ready for default use ("None of them are generally ready for use yet")
aarch64-macos and aarch64-windows still Tier 2, without CI parity with x86_64-linux's Tier 1
std.builtin.Type field renames break existing reflection/comptime code
@fence removed outright in favor of explicit atomic ordering barriers

os_support.windows: 10 (first release with an explicit "OS Version Requirements" minimum-version table)
os_support.freebsd: 14.0; dynamically-linked FreeBSD libc now supported when cross-compiling
os_support.netbsd: 10.1; dynamically-linked NetBSD libc now supported when cross-compiling

added: async/await keywords formally REMOVED from the language grammar (also @frameSize); "settled that there will not be async/await keywords in the language", to be replaced eventually by a std.Io interface
"Writergate": all-new std.Io.Writer/std.Io.Reader interfaces replacing the old generic writer/reader model
Incremental compilation reaches "stable enough" for -fno-emit-bin workflows
Threaded Codegen: semantic analysis, codegen, and linking can all run in parallel
LLVM 20; note: 0.15.0 itself was never released, 0.15.1 is the first build of this line
limitations: async/await no longer exists as language syntax; existing code must be rewritten by hand, no automatic migration
"Writergate" is a sweeping breaking change to nearly all I/O code (custom format methods now require "{f}"; format strings/options removed from format methods)
incremental compilation still experimental with "known bugs" that "can lead to miscompilations or incorrect compile errors"
Linux minimum jumped from 3.16 to 5.10, dropping support for older kernels
macOS minimum raised to 13.0
0.15.0 was never shipped publicly (only 0.15.1 and 0.15.2 patches exist)

os_support.solaris: none: support for Solaris (and AIX and z/OS) was REMOVED this release; illumos, as an open-source OpenSolaris fork, remains supported

added: std.Io interface: Future(T)/io.async/.await/.cancel task-level concurrency -- a colorblind-async-like model reintroducing async concepts as a library API rather than language syntax
std.Thread's higher-level sync primitives (Mutex, Condition, ResetEvent, WaitGroup, Futex, RwLock, Semaphore) gain std.Io.* equivalents
Windows networking without ws2_32.dll (NtDll migration completed)
heap.ArenaAllocator becomes thread-safe and lock-free by default
Basic support added for Alpha, KVX, MicroBlaze, OpenRISC, PA-RISC, SuperH (via the C backend with GCC, or an external LLVM/Clang fork only)
limitations: no HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 client (std.http remains HTTP/1.1-only); std.crypto.tls remains a TLS 1.3-only client with no server implementation
Io.Evented backend does not yet implement networking, and Io.net has no non-IP networking, so evented (single-threaded async) I/O and real networking cannot yet be combined
aarch64-macos and aarch64-windows remain Tier 2, still not Tier 1, roughly five years after Apple Silicon macOS support first appeared (0.8.0)
std.Thread.Pool removed outright; code depending on it must migrate to std.Io.Group/async
Solaris, AIX, and z/OS support removed entirely ("the Zig project cannot support proprietary operating systems that make it unreasonably difficult to obtain system headers")
heap.ThreadSafeAllocator removed
